comparator.name: History (Geschiedenis)
comparator.academicYear: Adopted 2026–2027 Dutch Geschiedenis OER, checked 2026-10-08; annual plans subject to change
comparator.sourceNotes: Adopted Dutch OER 2026–2027 annual plans pp. 22–23 establish one general route: first year 60 EC; second year 48 compulsory + two selected 6-EC choices; third year 30 minor/approved elective allowance + mandatory research college 9 + one selected global research seminar 9 + colloquium 3 + thesis 9. Total 180 EC. The first listed period-one/period-two choices are Capitalism and Inequality and Latin America in Modern History; other level-200 courses require prior examination-board permission. Mandatory Onderzoekscollege Cultuur, Religie en Kennis 500-1800 and the first-listed Research Seminar Global and Political History 1500-present are both taken; the alternative Global Economic and Social History seminar is not added. Genuine third-year profiling space remains generic, subject to approval and at least 12 EC at level 300 for an elective package. A university/faculty minor satisfying entry conditions is allowed under article 12.2; course overlap requires replacement approval. The alternatives abroad 30 or placement 12 plus electives 18 use the same allowance, not additional EC. The 0-EC Dutch language test is embedded in academic skills and not credited again. Research-college themes and annual plans may change. The English History and International Studies trajectory and its thesis codes are not substituted for the Dutch target.

routeSelection.basis: The Dutch Geschiedenis target uses its general Algemeen graduation direction, the broadest route, rather than a specialized direction or the distinct English History and International Studies trajectory. Second-year choices use the first listed 6-EC course in each period; the third-year extra research seminar uses the first listed alternative. No selection is based on UCR fit.

core: European and world history, empire, modernity and historical argument
Cultural history, public memory, heritage and historical sources
adjacent: Migration, war, state power and interpreting political violence
Globalisation, capitalism, inequality and environmental change

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: introduces markets, distribution and macroeconomic relationships needed to analyse the evidenced capitalism and globalisation direction
studies business cycles, goods and financial markets and policy effects as explanations of modern economic change
analyses incentives, strategic interaction and equilibrium as the economic mechanisms underlying the evidenced capitalism and inequality questions

develops research design and statistical inference for the evidenced quantitative-history and independent-research methods strand
surveys industrialisation, revolutions, world wars, decolonisation and European integration from 1815 to 2025

studies classical social theories in their historical imperial and colonial settings and interrogates the treatment of race and gender
practises qualitative interviewing and interpretation of situated social processes, complementing historical oral-source and research training

alternatives.label: History, cultural heritage & public memory
alternatives.concept: Study European and world historical change through written, oral, visual and material evidence, with substantive cultural heritage, public memory and historiography.
alternatives.labelReason: The label names the completed historical core and its actual companion disciplines; it does not claim the entire external period/geographic curriculum.
progression: All 24-course, 180-EC, level-300, PPD, exact semester-availability and hard-prerequisite checks passed. Foundational historical and social inquiry precedes final historical research; contemporary courses are explicitly related applications, not substitutes for period-specific historical modules. The six core History courses run in all alternatives. The research seminar is placed last; course-description-only evidence is identified where the enriched workbook has no outline.

alternatives.label: History, migration & political conflict
alternatives.concept: Study historical change through empire, warfare, migration, rights and political institutions, connecting historical sources with conflict and social-inclusion research.
alternatives.labelReason: The label names the completed historical core and its actual companion disciplines; it does not claim the entire external period/geographic curriculum.
progression: All 24-course, 180-EC, level-300, PPD, exact semester-availability and hard-prerequisite checks passed. alternatives.distinctness: The organising choice materially changes course selection: political theory, institutions, rights, peace/conflict and migrant inclusion replace the extensive art, museum and media-history sequence.

alternatives.label: History, political economy & global inequality
alternatives.concept: Study modern historical change through capitalism, globalisation, distribution and environmental struggles, combining historical inquiry with economic models and empirical social analysis.
alternatives.labelReason: The label names the completed historical core and its actual companion disciplines; it does not claim the entire external period/geographic curriculum.
progression: All 24-course, 180-EC, level-300, PPD, exact semester-availability and hard-prerequisite checks passed. Foundational historical and social inquiry precedes final historical research; contemporary courses are explicitly related applications, not substitutes for period-specific historical modules. The six core History courses run in all alternatives. The research seminar is placed last; course-description-only evidence is identified where the enriched workbook has no outline.
alternatives.distinctness: The organising choice materially changes course selection: five economic theory/methods courses and modern social theory replace specialist cultural study and much political-institution/conflict study. All pairwise differences are at least four courses / 30 EC; no substitutions were made merely to satisfy the numerical floor.

candidates.label: Migration, war and political conflict in historical perspective

selection.assessment: Three complete concepts pass evidence, coherence, substantive distinctness and mechanical feasibility: historical culture/public memory, migration/political conflict and global political economy. The second and third are related disciplinary responses grounded in the target’s actual interests and corrected requirements. Coverage does not claim a full Netherlands, medieval-Europe, Holocaust or Latin-American specialist sequence.

blocks: Both directly survey modern European history; UCR covers 1815–2025 and wider international developments.
The UCR course conducts and interprets oral interviews as part of gender history, directly addressing the external oral-history method; the subject and scope differ.
Both directly study historical change across world regions; UCR focuses on imperial rise and fall rather than the full chronological survey.
Both involve historical research on global/political relations; UCR uses primary sources about the 1809 multinational Walcheren expedition rather than the full external seminar range.
Both directly investigate ancient world societies through material evidence; UCR archaeology does not reproduce the complete Mediterranean historical survey.
Both directly study central texts and arguments in Western philosophy.
Both address early-modern European/Mediterranean cultural change; UCR focuses on Renaissance art and exchange, leaving the medieval and broader political sequence incomplete.
Both directly address inequality and capitalism’s distributive arrangements; UCR focuses on public economics and redistribution rather than the full historical account.
Both directly develop statistical analysis of human data; UCR supplies regression and multivariate inference in a contemporary human-data setting rather than the external historical applications.

notes.text: The UCR programmes support substantial historical inquiry with cultural, political or economic companion fields. VU additionally requires dedicated medieval/early-modern, Dutch, Holocaust/genocide, digital-history and selected regional research components that these UCR curricula do not reproduce.
